rv.q: “A Wonderful World: Armstrong Musical” is a majestic spectacle, paying homage to a towering figure and his distinctive legacy.
What we’re seeing on stage is too entertaining.

To showcase and to dissect always are tricky, twin ambitions for any jukebox show, and I think the main problem with “Wonderful World” is that it worries too much about the latter, which gets in the way of fully delivering the former.

Iglehart is aptly charming in this role — the modulations and mimicry of that iconic gravel is everything you want it to be — but charisma alone can only do so much to invigorate a plain script that too often skims over the complexities of Louis’ life as a Black artist in the early 20th century.
The show could be spectacular if only Armstrong were more active.
The musical offers a pleasing depiction of that joy and that mask, if not of those multitudes.

“A Wonderful World,” treating its title as purely ironic, does not sufficiently encompass that complexity; it’s vague because it cannot reconcile Armstrong’s overflowing affections (for women, music and people of all stripes) with the rigid absolutes of our time.
In the case of A Wonderful World, Louis Armstrong comes marching into Broadway aboard an overstuffed bio-musical.
What’s on Broadway is largely a deflating and cobbled-together wife story that fails to capture Armstrong, the artist.
A Wonderful World exceeds expectations and has enough pizzazz to be an exception to the rule.

A Wonderful World is an important story, a hopeful story with a sunny disposition, a story that believes in the possibility of change and in seeing the beauty in the world and trying to build a better one – with music and with love.

Iglehart winningly embodies a well-loved national figure, and A Wonderful World, directed by Christopher Renshaw and co-directed by Iglehart and Christina Sajous, benefits mightily from this, telling a story that, as a matter of the facts told, wasn’t all toothy smiles.

A Wonderful World, the biographical jukebox musical about the legendary jazz trumpeter and singer Louis Armstrong, is named for Armstrong’s signature song “What A Wonderful World.” But a more apt title might be “The Four Wives of Louis Armstrong” because each of the four actors portraying Armstrong...
Indeed, for all of its considerable entertainment value, “A Wonderful World” makes it hard for us to fully invest in Armstrong and the many people in his life.

The effort to do both does no particular favor to either.
But have we gotten to know Armstrong as a musician, husband, cultural force, his politics, his passion for music, his strengths and frailties?
Alas, as depicted in “A Wonderful World,” the late jazz giant comes across as puzzlingly smaller than life, or smaller than Armstrong’s life, at least.
As presented here, Armstrong is a talented and very amiable man whose only real direction in life is collecting a lot of wives, each of whom gets about 30 minutes on stage.

To say the least, it’s a lackluster concluding statement on the complexities of Armstrong’s marriages, as well as his feelings about a world that, despite all of its “trees of green” and “red roses too,” caused him so much pain.
A Wonderful World doesn’t offer a very deep understanding of Louis Armstrong and what made him a legend, but less can still be Satchmo.
This play is a great recreation of his music with terrific dancing, but it’s more vaudeville show than drama.

cn.t: Iglehart's remarkable Armstrong impersonation anchors this musically rich but overstuffed jukebox bio-musical. Critics praise the performances and jazz arrangements, but fault the wordy, unfocused book that struggles to find a cohesive narrative.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.'
